appraisal_events.evidence: "une bien sainte femme... qui ne plaignait pas les perdreaux, ni les faisans"; "s'il y a une femme qui peut compter d'aller près du bon Dieu, sûr et certain que c'est elle"; she starved herself so her servants could eat well.
appraisal_events.explanation: Françoise's extended reminiscence praises Mme Octave (tante Léonie) as saintly, boundlessly generous, and self-sacrificing, a judgment corroborated by the parish priest and unqualified by irony.

appraisal_events.evidence: An old friend of the narrator's father declares of the duchesse: "Elle a la plus grande situation dans le faubourg Saint-Germain, elle a la première maison du faubourg Saint-Germain."
appraisal_events.explanation: A witnessed outside testimony directly asserts the duchesse's supreme rank within the Faubourg Saint-Germain, reviving the prestige of the Guermantes name for the narrator.

appraisal_events.evidence: Watching her in the street or at her mirror, the narrator sees her follow fashion "comme si... elle avait aspiré à cette élégance... dans laquelle des femmes quelconques pouvaient l'égaler," admiring a well-dressed actress and fussing over her veil and sleeves "dans l'oubli mythologique de sa grandeur native."
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator's direct observation undercuts the mythic aura built around her name: seen in person she behaves with the vanity of an ordinary fashionable woman, like a queen forgetting she is divine to play a lesser role.

status_effects.explanation: Françoise's account leaves tante Léonie clearly elevated as an exemplary, generous, near-saintly mistress.
A witnessed outside testimony explicitly ranks her as holding the foremost position and household in the Faubourg Saint-Germain.

The narrator's private observation of her mundane vanity and fashion-consciousness deflates the mythic image built up by her name and reputation, though this judgment is not witnessed by others in the scene.
